newsitem.title: USA: Chip industry book-to-bill seen up at 0.94 or 0.95.
newsitem.headline: Chip industry book-to-bill seen up at 0.94 or 0.95.

text.p: Seeing renewed strength in demand for semiconductors, analysts expect the industry's book-to-bill ratio came close to a break-even number for September by rising to about 0.94 or 0.95.

The ratio, a leading indicator of future demand tallied by the industry's trade group, measures new orders against sales in a month. A 0.95 ratio would mean the chip industry got $95 worth of new orders for every $100 worth of chips it sold.
"It will show sequential improvement," said Mark Edelstone of Prudential Securities, adding it could be surprisingly good.
The U.S. Semiconductor Industry Association said it expects to report the September book-to-bill ratio on Tuesday.

Evidence that personal computer makers have sharply increased their orders for microprocessors and other chips built into PCs is one reason the book-to-bill will be up, analysts say, citing Intel Corp's sales outlook. PC makers are preparing for their biggest selling season, autumn.
Moreover, memory chip prices finally stopped falling in mid-September, analysts said, after an eight-month slide.
"It will be driven by PC demand and DRAM price improvements," said Dan Niles of Robertson, Stephens & Co.
Niles expects the ratio could hit 0.98, just short of break even, which would be 1.0.
PaineWebber analyst John Lazlo predicted a 0.95 September ratio and cited PC manufacturers' orders as the biggest influence.
Even at 0.95, the ratio would be higher than it has been all year.

But Prudential's Edelstone said he thinks there's a good chance the September ratio will top what most people estimate because of the influence of memory chip pricing. "Most of this year, DRAMs have been pressuring the ratio," he said.

Prices of memory chips, or DRAMs, plummeted over the course of the year to a fraction of what they were in January. Because memory chips make up about 40 percent of the unit volume of semiconductors shipped in a year, their prices have had a big influence on orders and sales measured in dollars.
But since mid-September, memory prices have risen 30 to 50 percent from their lows, Edelstone said. That gain could show up in either the September or October book-to-bill ratio.
Micron Technology Inc, the leading U.S. maker of memory chips, said late last week that memory chip inventories are down to desirable levels from formerly excessive levels.
Texas Instruments Inc is another big memory chip producer.

Although analysts expect a notable uptick in the September book-to-bill ratio, they caution that a higher ratio will not translate into higher third quarter semiconductor industry earnings. The book-to-bill, as a guage of orders, is a glimpse at future sales.

Lazlo said third quarter earnings reports could be the lowest of the year, with a few exceptions. Those exceptions are big suppliers to the PC industry, such as Adaptec Inc and S3 Inc along with Intel.
